utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances first, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I am Eric Ostberg. I appear today with Mr. Giuliano Turone, Ms. Teresa McHenry and Ms. Elles van Dusschoten. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The appearances for the defence? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I am Edina Residovic, defence counsel of Mr. Zejnil Delalic. With me in the team is Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor of Criminal Law from Canada. With us today also we have Mr. David Lee as our representative at this hearing. He is a lawyer from London. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, present for Esad Landzo today I am Cynthia McMurrey from the United States with Judge John Ackerman. Also in the gallery is the Honourable Mustafa Brackovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, allow me to introduce myself. I am Zeljko Olujic, an attorney from Croatia. I am defence counsel for Mr. Pavo Mucic. With me in the team is Mr. Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Welcome to the team, Mr. Olujic. We knew you were coming. You were approved as lead counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: If your Honours allow, as I have just joined the defence team, may I present three main reasons and strategic goals set out by the previous defence counsel, to which I should like to make a few corrections, if your Honours would allow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We will allow most things. I have read what I regard as your motion. Did you actually clear this with Mr. Greaves? Did you discuss it with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No, we have still not had time to discuss this, but these submissions have been given to the Trial Chamber, and that is the position of the new defence counsel, which differs from the strategy of the defence counsel up to the 16th of this month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I actually thought you would have discussed it with him since he has been in the matter even before you came in. Speaking for myself and for the Trial Chamber, an opening statement is not a very important part of the proceedings. You still have your time while the proceedings is going on to know how to determine your strategy, especially with very capable counsel in the chambers dealing with your matter. So I do not really see the basis for this opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Very well, your Honour. Thank you. MR. KARABDIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, my name is Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic. With me in the team is Mr. Tom Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Karabdic. I think that is where we stopped. Where do we continue today?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: As far as the prosecution is concerned, we are prepared to go on and have witnesses to call. On the other hand, I have understood already that there are some submissions from the defence before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us know exactly in what respect the submissions are being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I briefly address the Tribunal to explain the position that I occupy, and I will take a little time? May I say my name is David Lee. I was called to the Bar of England and Wales in 1973 and I am a member of Grays Inn in general practice in chambers in London. I specialise in criminal law. I have been instructed to advise Ms. Edina Residovic and Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I just want to inform the Trial Chamber that the matter that is now going to be taken up is the one we discussed in private session the last time we were sitting. Just for the sake of caution I put that before your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, I only want to know the basis of the submissions, because it has to be on a matter before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: It has to do with the position of defence counsel in relation to the proposed hearing this afternoon. For my part, I would have thought, since the discussions out of which it arises were conducted in closed session, that it may be more appropriate for my remarks to be made in closed session than open, and I believe that that would be concurred in by the prosecution and probably others who may or may not know of the basis of it. As an excess of caution I would ask your Honour to consider going into closed session for a short time, so that I can explain my position here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Now before you go on, our last closed session discussion terminated the participation of this Trial Chamber in that matter, because we said we are referring the matter to the President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: I entirely agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: At the end of those proceedings we were no longer involved in what is going on in that discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: I entirely accept that. It has to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Do I not see how you come into that type of discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: It has to do, your Honour, with respect, with regard to the personal position of the defence advocates in relation to the continued proceedings this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you counsel in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am instructed on behalf of those persons individually. I have no instructions, nor do I seek them, in relation to any Defendant before these proceedings in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: None of them is an accused person before us or a defendant before the Trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: As I have indicated, it is certainly my application, and I know that both of the lawyers who I have mentioned were anxious that I indicate to the Trial Chamber their personal professional positions with regard to these proceedings. As I have indicated, it seems to me appropriate that will be done in closed session with regard to the fact that it does -- the decision of referral on 16th May provides the background to what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I hope you have not misunderstood me. What I said at the conclusion of that proceeding that day and we decided to refer that matter to the President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: I understand that fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We became functus officio as far as that was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: I accept that entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not know how in this regard this Trial Chamber will go into that matter again. What I understand is you suggest in continuing proceedings counsel would still want to be represented in their reluctance to continue. This is the argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: I will explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I see that, but my predicament is that you are not a counsel in these proceedings and any of them could have made a statement indicating what he wants.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: I accept that, but the position is simply this, as I understand it. My professional clients are entitled in circumstances such as this to seek independent advice, which they have done, with regard to their own positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: Professionally and otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: When the accused are in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: As a matter of courtesy they have instructed me to apply for leave from this Trial Chamber to explain very briefly to the Trial Chamber their position which they have reached with regard to their professional decision with regard to their position, having regard to the continuing calling of evidence in relation to this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please do not misunderstand me. I am not trying to be difficult. I am trying to be purely formal about what we are doing. As far as our rules go, this might be the first time counsel appearing before us for the accused persons have also enlisted other counsel to appear on their behalf. Now we have no provision for any other counsel appearing other than counsel appearing on behalf of the accused persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: Well, certainly I would accept entirely that any participation which I would seek to have in this Trial Chamber but for the fact that it is to explain to the Trial Chamber the personal position of those who have instructed me, that is to say the lawyers themselves, I entirely, with respect, agree entirely with what your Honour says, but in my submission the position here is quite different. I am here not to intervene in regard to the proceedings themselves. I am merely here to hopefully illustrate a decision which has been made by my clients in respect of their continued participation at this particular stage of the Tribunal business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I am afraid we have always tried to make it clear that we do not want to be involved in these other proceedings, being the Trial Chamber before which this matter is going on. Whatever you will now say will appear to be getting us into the whole exercise. When the President comes in, you might be able to represent anybody you want to there, but I see nothing insidious in any counsel who does not want to continue with the proceedings because of this difficulty in saying so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I see nothing, because it is counsel's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Counsel's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: May I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Because whatever submission anyone has, he is free to make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: Of course. May I say, your Honour, the position is quite clear. I want to make it quite clear that, in fact, both Ms. Residovic and Mr. O'Sullivan felt that it was a matter of actual courtesy to the Tribunal that what they had to say was said on their behalf by myself, because of the serious position and the serious decision which they had taken as a result of this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: My fear, as I told you, I am not sure you have a locus here. I am not too sure, because you have to be representing someone, which as far as I know you are not, because those whom you claim to represent are not accused persons before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: I accept that. I accept that. Of course, I am in your Honour's hands. I do not purport to represent any Defendant in these proceedings, as your Honour knows, and I am entirely in the Tribunal's hands, as I have indicated, I hope quite clearly. The position that I had sought to adopt I have made clear, I hope, and I respectfully apply to be heard on their behalf at their request in closed session to explain the decision they have taken, but I am entirely in the Tribunal's hands, of course, as to whether the Tribunal grants me leave to be heard on that matter and that matter alone. On that basis I will be repeating again, and repetition never increases the force of an argument, I am in the Tribunal's hands as to whether or not I should be heard in that capacity or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think I will repeat this, that if these are proceedings of the Trial Chamber in respect of the matters involving these accused persons, I do not see how your locus comes in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: Well, it has to do with the fact that I think that I can be quite blunt and say if the Trial Chamber proceeds to hear evidence from witnesses regarding the business before the Trial Chamber, my present instructions are that in relation to both Ms. Residovic and Mr. O'Sullivan that they feel professionally precluded from acting on behalf of Mr. Delalic at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: May I say something? I hope you read the closing observations of the Chamber on the last occasion --

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: -- the Chamber met. Maybe the incident has nothing to do with the Tribunal at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why should counsel feel hesitant because we said something that is no cloud on anyone, so they can carry on their function without any fear, without any sort of hesitation altogether. I do not think it is really necessary to go into this matter at this stage. Let the inquiry be held. Maybe this has nothing to do with the Tribunal at all, including the defence counsel. In fact, the article in question had itself indicated the source from which it could have obtained information, and it is entirely outside the Tribunal. Why should counsel be hesitant? Why should they feel a little handicapped in any way?

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: May I say that I understand fully that everyone in this room proceeds on the basis it has nothing whatsoever to do with defence counsel and that is entirely accepted and entirely understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it would be fair if you define your status in relation to the Trial Chamber. Just let us know how you come to be counsel in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: As I have indicated before, I was instructed personally by Mr. O'Sullivan and Ms. Residovic in their personal capacity. I do not seek nor do I claim any right of ordinance beyond that. As I say, I repeat myself if I go beyond that. The position is simply this. I have had responsibility, however, to advise them in respect of certain professional matters which arise out of the fact, and I accept entirely it has nothing to do with this Trial Chamber, but the referred complaint of a seriousness which it is hard to say -- one could not see it being more serious than it is, has nonetheless left them in a position where, until that matter is resolved, acting, as they must do on behalf of their Defendant fearlessly and without favour and without concern for personal position, they nonetheless perceive a potential -- I say potential, not actual -- a potential conflict of interest that has arisen. That conflict, may I say, is very likely to be completely removed at the end of the investigation, which I anticipate the President may or may not call into this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: One has granted you audience out of courtesy purely because, as I said, I do not see how they become accused persons or how they become defendants, in which respect they needed counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: There is no question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If they are not, then why do you have Defendant and counsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why should you presume the odium will fall on them? The enquiry is not even held. In fact, it is found later on the defence and the Tribunal has nothing to do with that, it will be all wasted time. Why do you presume there will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: If I may say so, that is completely understood. They are in no way treating themselves in that position, but the reality is in relation to this counsel's duty, as one perceives their position, is also to consider, however the scope for potential conflict which may arise. This is the point which they are making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If they had analysed the position properly, analysed the legal implications of the facts, perhaps you would have come in at a later stage, at a stage they are sure there is anything to defend, not now, when all you want to do is to announce to the Trial Chamber certain things. This is not important, because you are in no way concerned with the proceedings of this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: As far as I am concerned there is a procedure for getting counsel on the Trial Chamber. I am not sure -- nothing has been referred to me about your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: I have attempted in the short time available to me to attempt to comply with the formal requirements as best I could, and I have also tried to make it clear as best I could out of courtesy the position, which I hope the Trial Chamber will understand is not an easy one for someone in my position to adopt. I preface all my remarks by saying it probably sounded very discourteous of me to introduce it in this way, but I hope it is understood to be as courteous as I could be to the Tribunal to indicate the position I am instructed to adopt. My position is simply this: having regard to the fact and as anticipated by both of the clients who have instructed me, it is anticipated by them that they are in no way suspected directly or indirectly by anyone, anticipated entirely, but nonetheless the position that I was simply to make clear was they nonetheless until the resolution of that matter in relation to their client and themselves and, indeed, everyone else who is a potential source of investigation has been dealt with, which in our respectful submission would be a relatively short time, until such time as that, they find themselves professionally embarrassed with regard to conducting cross-examination of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not going into the details. I am only saying it would be improper for me to accept you as counsel to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is what I am saying, because I have tried --

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: -- to make you realise that that is the order. If you are counsel to anybody, obviously you have all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: I am very grateful to the court for that indication. Unless I can assist the court further, those are, therefore, my submissions before it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It would be improper for me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I have other reasons for doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LEE
utterances.text: Of course. I am grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Residovic? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, we tried to convey through our legal representative our decision, Mr. O'Sullivan's and mine. I apologise if this was not the proper way in which to inform the Trial Chamber of this. However, in view of the discussion we had in this Trial Chamber twice and the decision of the Trial Chamber, as well as the fact that the Prosecutor must carry out a certain inquiry that we discussed on Friday, as professional lawyers we have decided that out of deeply ethical and professional reasons we can no longer participate in these proceedings as defence counsel of Mr. Zejnil Delalic until the problem, which will be heard elsewhere, has been dealt with. The possibility of a potential conflict of interest between us and our client and in both in the interest of our client and in the interests of our professional and ethical considerations does not allow us to continue participating in the presentation of evidence in this Trial Chamber, because we deeply respect the Trial Chamber and we would not like our position in any way under any circumstances to call in question the fairness of the proceedings in this trial as well as the position of our client in these proceedings. That is why I once again, on behalf of Mr. O'Sullivan and myself, apologise if our legal representative expressed himself, or rather following our instructions presented our position in a way that was not the most suitable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): I apologise. Also let me just add one further phrase. Your Honours, when this problem has been fully settled we are fully prepared to continue to represent our client. Should the decision of the court be in a different vein, then it will be up to our client to choose another defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I am proud to listen to you and I believe my colleagues, too, are very happy to hear your own submission and the reasons why you have taken that position. In addition to the undertaking which even the Prosecutor has made, the Trial Chamber has the highest regard for all counsel appearing before us, and would never for one moment think that you have anything to do with it, but since this is a matter which one can point fingers at, I think we believe as professionals you are right to indicate where your mind is going, and there is nothing anyone can do about it than to ensure that you keep to your professional ethics and make sure that your loyalty to justice, which is the main thing here, and this is what everyone is looking forward to in the whole exercise, is maintained, and also that your integrity above everything is sustained throughout. We believe you have done the right thing and I think on behalf of my colleagues we admire the position you have taken. As I said on Friday, when the President comes, and I hear he is coming tomorrow, every effort will be made to set the machinery in motion so that this whole thing will be cleared up and the situation will never be as cloudy as it now appears to be. In all the circumstances I believe the prosecution will still tell you that whatever it is it still regards your cooperation with him as the best thing he has ever had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I do not see any conflict between your interests and your client. This is nothing to do at all with your interest and your client's interest. How can they come into conflict? I just do not understand. Somebody has leaked information to the Press. No one from the tribunal, including defence counsel has anything to do with it. The only thing is blowing the incident out of proportion by saying you cannot possibly represent your client because there is a conflict. I just do not understand that. I do not see the conflict at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I assist your Honours? I know something of the background of the decision that counsel have made? Of course, welcoming things have been said by counsel for the prosecution, which have been helpful to indicate their present position, but let us suppose for a moment that we now continue with this trial and a parallel inquiry begins behind the scenes, and during the course of that inquiry, and I will be careful, because I know that we are in open session, someone is interviewed and makes an allegation, which raises a suspicion against counsel. That is the first problem. The second problem is that something may happen in relation to the Defendant during the course of his being interviewed which may raise the same sort of problem. I know that if I was acting in their position, if I had constantly between now and the conclusion of the inquiry that must take place, to be worried about that, and the situation had not yet been resolved completely, I would not feel able to concentrate and to focus upon the interests of my client if I was having to worry in any way about my own position. The duty of counsel at the Bar is this: to defend his client fearlessly and without favour within the rules of his profession. If he is in any way prohibited from so doing, then that is not in the interests either of his client or of justice, because if one is concerned and is in some way -- has one's ability to follow your duty impinged upon, then you cannot do that which is in the interests of your client. That is the first point. The second point is this. Let us say we come to the end of this trial and Mr. Delalic found himself in the situation where he was going to have to appeal against a conviction. One of the grounds might be: "For a period of two weeks", let us say, "while this enquiry was going on, my counsel, their mind was not properly on the job, because there was this background of an enquiry". That might prove to be a very sound and fundamental ground of an appeal, that for two critical weeks his counsel were not able properly to carry out their duty on his behalf. That is why in the interests of justice, in my submission, this trial should not continue until such time as the position is entirely, and I stress entirely, clear. Your Honour's words are most kind about my learned colleagues that there is no suspicion upon them as far as your Honours are concerned, and that is a most welcome approbation, if I may say so, and all of us feel heartened by them. There are ramifications, and the word "potential" comes in here. One knows only too well in an enquiry of this kind things go in an unexpected direction. We cannot look into a crystal ball and say with certainty: "This will happen, this will happen and this will happen". Something may arise during that enquiry which has a fundamental effect on the way in which it goes and the way in which counsel for Delalic are viewed either by the Tribunal or the prosecution. Whilst they are worrying about that and have that in the back of their minds, they cannot properly conduct the defence of their client. If that is the position, a serious injustice would arise to the Defendant Delalic. They have plainly considered their position, and it is plainly expressed that their decision is that they cannot within the terms of their ethics continue to represent their client pro tempore with this problem in the background. The consequences of that are these, as I understand what they have said: they feel it incumbent on them to withdraw from these proceedings until such time as they are cleared. That means that the defendant Delalic is without counsel. In my respectful submission he cannot and this trial cannot continue if he is unrepresented. He is entitled to counsel of his choice. For the time being for ethical reasons his counsel cannot properly act and, that being so, with respect your Honours are faced with something of a fait accompli, that the reality is this trial cannot continue until the inquiry is commenced and finished. This means this: that inquiry has to be got underway expeditiously in everyone's interests, not least that of counsel who act for Mr. Delalic. That is going to require the prosecution to move swiftly, and I suspect it is in their interests as well to move swiftly in order to bring that inquiry to an end and a conclusion to be reached. But my submission is this: this trial cannot properly continue if the decision of Ms. Residovic and Mr. O'Sullivan is, for perfectly proper and sound, if I may say so, professional reasons, if they cannot continue for the time being to represent Mr. Delalic. The answer is this trial cannot continue. This is a serious matter that has been raised. It is not one that is peripheral and can be dealt with, as seems happens, at the end of a trial. This is a problem that goes to the very root, not just of these proceedings but, I suspect, as far as the prosecution are concerned, to the very root of the entire process that this Tribunal has been set up to deal with. In my submission, although superficially attractive that we can continue and this inquiry can go on, the reality is that it cannot, and what I am trying to say to your Honours is that there is a little bit more to it than simply: "Well, set up an inquiry and everything will be all right." I am afraid it is not as simple as that. The position I have laid out, because of the professional considerations of counsel for Mr. Delalic, means, I regret, and I regret it greatly, but it is an inevitable consequence of what I say, this trial cannot properly continue. I do not know if there is anything I can assist by way of explanation of what I have said to your Honours, but I hope I have made the position as clear as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Can we hear the Prosecutor on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. The prosecution has heard the decision put forward by Madam Residovic on her own and on Mr. O'Sullivan's behalf, and I would like to quote your Honour saying: "There is nothing anybody can do about it." I respect it and I regret it and I have no other wish in this trial but to go swiftly and expeditiously. We have a witness waiting, etc, etc, but we have been put in a situation about which I can do nothing. Just to answer Mr. Greaves, it is not the prosecution who is going to make enquiries. It is the President or anybody he would name. I will do all, if it is anything in my power to do so, to make that work swiftly, but I think -- I have the strongest respect for Ms. Residovic and Mr. O'Sullivan's standpoint. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It has been very sad for the Trial Chamber to accept this decision, now we know it is on professional grounds, we cannot challenge the judgment of professionals who think and consider duly that they are protecting their integrity and also they are trying to work in the interests of justice. It is in this matter that we have had a lot of anxiety from the accused persons, who want speedy trials, and from accused persons who have quite varied types of complaints about the proceedings and how speedily we are carrying them out, and everyone thought that we could have been spared this problem of having to delay any further when, in fact, we could have carried on. Now the question of justice is a very important thing and, as judges, we are merely impartial arbiters and we make sure we protect the interest of everybody involved, accused person, counsel, Prosecutor, and we ensure that at all costs nobody should suffer for the misdeeds of any other person. So I think in this circumstance if counsel is convinced, and I think here they are convinced, that it would not be in their interests to continue while a parallel investigation is going on, although we differ, I think their judgment ought to be respected. I think we hope that this inquiry will be pursued very vigorously and speedily so that we will waste very minimum time in staying away. As I said, it is very sad, but I hope it is not dragging the skirmish from somewhere into our Trial Chamber. I think this is all I have to say about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only thing we could ask for is for the Trial Chamber to set up as early as is convenient a time for a status conference to see where we stand and how long this will go on, if the Trial Chamber will find that a reasonable thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That might be fairly difficult in the circumstance. Let me hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. If we are moving forward from that so it is not a total waste of time, and by no means am I saying that this is a waste of time, but I have spoken to Ms. Theresa McHenry on Friday. They have witness M who is waiting here to testify, who has alleged serious bodily injuries arising out of this case, and many times the medical examination of the witness takes place after he testifies. So we have not gotten an answer on that issue yet, but we are asking that this witness, since he is here in The Hague, if he could be examined ahead of time before he testifies, that will certainly finish all the testimony for that witness if he finally gets to testify. If we can get that arranged, it would certainly expedite the rest of the trial also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually I do not know what part of the proceedings that will be. That portion is taken up now, I do not know what portion of our proceedings it will be.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Sometimes it could be that once a witness has testified and then the medical examination comes afterwards, there may be a reason to have to recall that witness at a later time. If we have the medical examination before the witness testifies, then there would be no need and everything would be presented at the time the witness testifies. That is all we are asking. Ms. McHenry said she was going to check on that. I am sure we could probably have that done before this witness testifies now. That is all I am asking. I would like to try to get that resolved ahead of time since we have time now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Assuming your Honours want the Prosecution to respond to this, Ms. McMurrey did raise this and I said I would check with lead counsel and the witness. The prosecution is willing to support a joint application to the Trial Chamber requesting a medical examination. It has been agreed by defence counsel and I assume by all defence counsel that in any cases where a joint application is made for a medical examination the actual report can come into evidence to your Honours as joint exhibits. I believe this has been -- we have had this issue come up before with respect to our witnesses. So as long as that is clear that the medical examination of this witness and the other witnesses can be admitted into evidence as a joint exhibit by all parties to assist the truth finding process, we would support a joint application to have this witness, witness M, receive a medical examination at your Honour's direction. Presumably you would ask that the Registrar appoint, as I believe your Honours did with respect to the first two witnesses, that your Honours asked the Registrar to appoint an impartial medical expert, and then it is just a matter of with respect to the Victim Witness Unit how quickly that can be arranged. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, we have received three other medical reports on three previous witnesses to this point, and we stipulate that we agree that they will be admissible. If the same procedures are followed for this witness, we would also do the same. I assume that the same proceedings procedures will be followed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just very briefly address the primary issue that has brought us to this point? I am distressed by the delay that we seem to be facing, and perhaps I am trying to speak to the President through this Trial Chamber, but it seems to me that if the enquiry can immediately and quickly focus upon the issue of whether or not any counsel bear any responsibility for any of the activities we discussed last week that it is very likely that in a very, very, very short period of time the President or whoever he appoints to carry out those tasks could announce that there is absolutely no evidence to support any such allegations against counsel in this case. That to me would remove the ethical issues and this trial could go forward. So hopefully that enquiry could be in two phases, the first phase enquiring whether any counsel bear any responsibility. I think that can be dealt with quickly, and then we can move forward. I dread that we might be looking at an extended period of time while a very broad-based inquiry goes on. I think it can be handled in a much briefer and much simpler way with regard to counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ackerman. I think we would not want to stay indefinitely. The President will be here tomorrow. We will leave out tomorrow and assemble here again at 10 o'clock on Thursday, so that we might know how things go. I think we will assemble here on Thursday at 10.00 am. So the Trial Chamber will now rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: --ooOoo--

procedural_notes.text: (Hearing adjourned until 10.00 am on Thursday morning)
